prompt.context: Your client is a pharmaceutical company called US Pharma. They just received FDA approval for a new anti-depressant drug that is expected to become a big hit for the company. A previous market study shows that demand will be very high for this new drug. Therefore, US Pharma will have to either expand its current factory in Texas or build a new one in Virginia, closer to the port.
prompt.question: How will you approach this problem and help your client make a decision about whether to expand the Texas facility or build a new facility in Virginia?

clarifying_info.q: What other products does US Pharma sell?
clarifying_info.a: The company sells many kinds of drugs in the US and Europe (their second largest market). The new drug is also approved for sale in Europe. Focus only on the new anti-depressant drug; the other drugs are not important for this case.

clarifying_info.q: What is the investment required for each option?
clarifying_info.a: Expanding the Texas facility costs $36M; building a new Virginia facility costs $50M.

clarifying_info.q: What is the expected demand and pricing?
clarifying_info.a: Demand is 10,000,000 pills in the US and 5,000,000 pills in Europe. Average price per pill is $2 in the US and $3 in Europe.
Texas: $50,000 per year per employee. Virginia: 10% lower than Texas. Both plants will need 100 employees.

clarifying_info.q: What are the raw material (compound) costs?
clarifying_info.a: Compound A: $0.10 per pill; Compound B: $0.70 per pill; Compound C: $0.20 per pill. Total compounds: $1.00 per pill.

clarifying_info.q: What is the production cost per pill?
clarifying_info.a: $0.50 per pill, same for both options.
Texas: 10% of compound cost. Virginia: 5% of compound cost (all compounds are imported and enter the US through the Virginia port).

clarifying_info.q: What are the depreciation, tax, and cost-of-capital assumptions?
clarifying_info.a: Straight-line depreciation; total investment fully depreciated in 10 years. Tax rate: 33% for both options. Cost of capital: 10% per year. No change in working capital or capex. Assume this year's earnings repeat in perpetuity.

framework: Define the decision objective: choose the option with the higher Net Present Value (NPV)
Structure the financial model: Revenue – Costs = Operating Profit → Net Earnings → Free Cash Flow → NPV
Revenue: identical for both options (same drug, same markets, same prices)
Cost buckets to compare: (1) Labor, (2) Raw materials / compounds, (3) Production, (4) Inbound logistics, (5) SG&A, (6) Depreciation
Apply taxes to get net earnings; add back depreciation to get free cash flow
Calculate NPV = FCF / Cost of Capital – Initial Investment
Recommend the option with the higher NPV; then brainstorm qualitative benefits

questions.prompt: Calculate annual revenue for US Pharma's new anti-depressant drug.
questions.guidance: Revenue is the same for both factory options since selling prices and volumes are identical. US revenue: $2 × 10M pills = $20M. Europe revenue: $3 × 5M pills = $15M. Total revenue = $35M.

math.setup: Revenue = (US price × US volume) + (Europe price × Europe volume)

questions.prompt: Calculate annual costs for the Texas option and the Virginia option separately.
questions.guidance: Walk through each cost line. Key differences are labor (Virginia is 10% cheaper), inbound logistics (Virginia is 5% vs Texas 10%), and depreciation (Virginia investment is higher). All other costs are identical.

math.setup: Total pills = 10M + 5M = 15M. Compound cost per pill = $0.10 + $0.70 + $0.20 = $1.00. Total compound cost = $1.00 × 15M = $15M.

questions.prompt: Calculate net earnings (after tax) for each option.
questions.guidance: Operating profit = Revenue – Total costs. Apply 33% tax rate to get net earnings. Note that Virginia has lower pre-tax profit despite lower labor and logistics costs because of higher depreciation from the larger upfront investment.

math.setup: Net earnings = Operating profit × (1 – tax rate)

questions.prompt: Calculate free cash flow (FCF) for each option.
questions.guidance: FCF = Net earnings + Depreciation – Change in working capital – Capex. Working capital change and Capex are both zero per the case assumptions. Depreciation must be added back — if the candidate forgets this, both options show negative NPV.

math.setup: FCF = Net earnings + Depreciation (WC change = 0, Capex = 0)

questions.prompt: Calculate NPV for each option and make a recommendation.
questions.guidance: Use the perpetuity formula: NPV = FCF / Cost of Capital – Initial Investment. Despite Virginia's higher annual FCF, the larger upfront investment results in a lower NPV. Texas has the higher NPV and is therefore the recommended choice.

math.setup: NPV = (FCF / Cost of capital) – Initial investment; Cost of capital = 10%
math.answer: NPV: Texas = $14.4M; Virginia = $13.4M → Recommend expanding the Texas facility

brainstorming.prompt: Besides having the highest NPV, what other benefits may US Pharma gain by choosing to expand the Texas facility?

categories.name: Revenue side
ideas: Faster time to market: expanding an existing facility is typically quicker than building a new one, allowing US Pharma to launch and capture customers sooner
First-mover advantage: reaching the market faster can secure customer loyalty and brand recognition before competitors enter

categories.name: Cost side
ideas: Distribution synergies: US Pharma can leverage existing distribution relationships and logistics networks used for its other drugs, reducing marginal distribution costs
Production synergies: existing Texas operations may share equipment, processes, or know-how with the new drug, reducing per-unit production costs
Economies of scale in procurement: US Pharma may negotiate better pricing on compounds by bundling purchases with existing supplier relationships for its other drugs

recommendation: US Pharma should expand its existing facility in Texas
The Texas expansion yields a higher NPV ($14.4M vs $13.4M for Virginia), driven by the lower initial investment ($36M vs $50M) that more than offsets Virginia's modest operating cost advantages
risks: Capacity risk: expanding an existing facility may face physical or zoning constraints that limit future scale
Concentration risk: housing production for multiple drugs in one Texas facility increases exposure to a single-site disruption (e.g., natural disaster, labor action)
Virginia upside ignored: if European demand grows significantly, proximity to the Virginia port could become increasingly valuable and erode the Texas NPV advantage
next_steps: Confirm construction timeline and feasibility for the Texas expansion to ensure it can meet the drug's launch schedule
Assess whether the Texas facility has sufficient long-term capacity headroom for potential demand growth
Model sensitivity of NPV to key assumptions (drug price, volume, cost of capital) to stress-test the recommendation
